vignette: Mark is a 21-year-old European-American male who has recently been struggling with the aftermath of witnessing a traumatic event involving his family. The incident involved a sudden and violent confrontation in which Mark’s father was severely injured. This event has left him feeling deeply unsettled and overwhelmed by intrusive memories and heightened threat perceptions. Ever since that fateful day, Mark has found himself hyper-vigilant to perceived threats, particularly when he notices people acting suspiciously or hears comments about his family. These triggers not only make him feel on guard but also lead him to avoid certain situations, such as watching TV programmes or films that remind him of the event. He had come to believe that these media representations would only exacerbate his anxiety and retraumatize him. The traumatic memory is particularly vivid for Mark; he can smell the same scents from that day whenever he thinks about it, and the images are like photographs in his mind. This photographic recall has made it nearly impossible for him to put the event into words, which leaves him feeling isolated and unable to express what he’s going through. He often relives those moments, suddenly feeling as if the traumatic experience were happening again, which further intensifies his feelings of danger. Mark had begun avoiding being alone in a room or building, fearing that sudden movements by others could immediately put him on guard. His body reacts as if he is still in danger even when he knows rationally that he is safe, and this has left him feeling like his body is an enemy rather than a source of comfort. He is also certain that he is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him—his confidence shaken to its core. His sleep problems have worsened as well; he struggles to fall or stay asleep due to constant worry and the persistent threat he feels even in his own home. The heightened sense of danger has led Mark to self-harm, a behavior he engages in to release overwhelming feelings that seem otherwise uncontrollable. This cycle of self-harm and avoidance only reinforces his negative appraisals about himself—feeling unable to rely on himself or manage his emotions effectively. The memories that haunt him are so vivid that they often push him further into these maladaptive strategies, as he feels trapped by both the past and present fears. When he is alone, he cannot shake off the intrusive thoughts, and this exacerbates his feelings of helplessness and inability to cope with daily life. Mark’s relationships have also been affected; being unemployed makes it difficult for him to engage in activities that might provide some distraction or support. He has become increasingly isolated from his friends and family, finding that even small comments about his loved ones can trigger intense distress. The combination of these symptoms has created a self-reinforcing cycle where Mark’s negative appraisals about himself and the world lead to increased triggers, which in turn heighten his sense of threat. He had come to believe that he cannot rely on himself anymore, making it even more challenging for him to seek help or engage in activities that might provide relief. What frightens Mark most is the idea that he will never be able to escape this loop and return to a life where he feels safe and capable. Despite his current state of isolation and distress, he still hopes to find some way to regain control over his emotions and live a more fulfilling life without the constant fear and reliving of the traumatic event. The trauma has left him feeling deeply vulnerable and disconnected from the world around him, but he is determined to seek help and break free from this cycle.
